title: Hymn to Intellectual Beauty: composition and publication
short: Written in summer 1816 near Lake Geneva, printed in Hunt's Examiner (19 January 1817) and reprinted with Rosalind and Helen (1819).
body: Shelley composed the Hymn in the summer of 1816 in Switzerland, during the months spent near Byron on Lake Geneva; the period also produced 'Mont Blanc'. He sent a fair copy to Leigh Hunt, who lost it, and a second copy was published in The Examiner on 19 January 1817; it was reprinted in the Rosalind and Helen volume (1819). A further fair copy in Mary Shelley's hand was found in 1976 in the 'Scrope Davies notebook', with substantial variants. The poem is a religious 'hymn' addressed to a non-religious power, a secular sceptic's devotional ode; critics stress the influence of Wordsworth's Immortality Ode and Rousseau's Julie, ou la Nouvelle Héloïse, which Shelley read on the same trip.

title: awful shadow of some unseen Power
short: An awe-inspiring but invisible power, known only by its passing 'shadow' on human experience.
body: 'Awful' keeps its older sense of 'awe-inspiring', not 'very bad'. The Power is never seen directly; only its 'shadow' visits us, and even that 'floats though unseen'. Shelley's language is deliberately tentative ('some'), refusing to name a deity. The Platonic resonance is strong (shadows of a higher reality, as in the cave of Republic 7), though Shelley read the Symposium only in August 1817 and the Phaedrus in 1818, after the Hymn was written, and Barrell argued that the poem is not strictly Platonic. 'Power' also links the Hymn to 'Mont Blanc', written in the same summer.

title: with as inconstant wing / As summer winds
short: The Power visits irregularly and unpredictably, like a breeze moving from flower to flower.
body: The first stanza is a chain of similes (summer winds, moonbeams, hues and harmonies of evening, clouds, remembered music), each describing something fleeting, delicate and beautiful. The accumulation itself conveys the elusiveness of the Power, which can only be approached by analogy. 'Inconstant' introduces the poem's central problem: the visitations are intermittent, and the speaker cannot command their return.

title: The stanza
short: Seven irregular twelve-line stanzas, rhyming abbaaccbddee, with varying line lengths and a long fifth line.
body: Each of the seven stanzas has twelve lines with the same rhyme scheme (abbaaccbddee) and the same pattern of line lengths, mixing pentameters, shorter tetrameter lines and a long fifth line that swells to six stresses (here 'Like moonbeams that behind some piny mountain shower'). The pattern loosely recalls the Pindaric or irregular ode tradition and the stanza of Wordsworth's Immortality Ode, while the title calls it a 'hymn'. The shortening lines in the middle of each stanza produce an effect of breath catching or flickering, suited to the inconstant visitations described.

title: Spirit of BEAUTY / Intellectual Beauty
short: The title's 'intellectual' means non-material, perceived by the mind; the hymn to Beauty recalls Spenser's Fowre Hymnes.
body: 'Intellectual' here means belonging to the realm of the intellect or spirit as opposed to the senses, an older philosophical sense derived from Platonism (OED). The title evokes Spenser's Fowre Hymnes (1596), which include 'An Hymne in Honour of Beautie' and 'An Hymne of Heavenly Beautie', Renaissance Neoplatonic praises of beauty as the reflection of the divine. Shelley borrows the form of devotional address but withholds belief in a God behind the Beauty. The capitals (BEAUTY, LOVELINESS, SPIRIT) mark the moments of direct invocation.

title: dost consecrate
short: To make sacred; the Spirit sanctifies whatever it lights upon, a religious word for a secular experience.
body: 'Consecrate' (Latin consecrare, to make holy) belongs to the language of worship: the Spirit hallows whatever human thought or form it shines upon. The verb sets the pattern of the poem, which repeatedly borrows religious vocabulary (hymn, vow, dedicate, worship, spells) to describe an experience that rejects orthodox religion. Shelley echoes Wordsworth's 'The consecration, and the Poet's dream' ('Elegiac Stanzas', Peele Castle, 1807, l. 16).

title: This dim vast vale of tears
short: The world as a place of sorrow: a phrase from Christian devotion, ultimately from Psalm 84.
body: 'Vale of tears' translates the Latin lacrimarum valle of the Salve Regina, a medieval Marian prayer, and derives from the 'valley of Baca' (weeping) in Psalm 84:6 (Psalm 83:7 in the Vulgate numbering), rendered in the Latin Vulgate as 'valle lacrimarum'. The phrase became proverbial for earthly life as exile and suffering. Shelley uses Christian words to describe the condition of life when the Spirit is absent, without the Christian promise of a heavenly home. The long fifth line enlarges the sense of desolation.

title: the names of Demon, Ghost, and Heaven
short: Names invented by sages and poets to explain experience are mere records of failure; Shelley revised this line after its first printing.
body: No revelation from 'some sublimer world' has answered the questions of stanza 2; therefore the words religion and superstition supply (demon, ghost, heaven) merely record 'vain endeavour'. Line 27 is one of two lines (with l. 58) that Shelley corrected after the Examiner printing, and the Scrope Davies copy differs from the printed texts in many places, so editors compare the early witnesses; the archive follows the Rosalind and Helen text. 'Demon' may carry the Greek sense of daimon, an intermediary spirit, rather than devil. Editors (Reiman and Fraistat; the Longman editors) discuss the variants.

title: Frail spells
short: These names are charms or incantations too weak to separate human life from doubt, chance and change.
body: Religious names are reduced to magic 'spells' whose 'uttered charm' cannot 'sever' doubt, chance and mutability from what we perceive. The word is ironic, since at the end of the poem the Spirit itself is said to have bound the poet with 'spells' (l. 83): Shelley replaces one enchantment with another, but one that operates through feeling and not dogma.

title: Doubt, chance, and mutability
short: The three conditions of mortal life; 'mutability' (changeableness) was a theme Shelley had treated in a lyric of the same name.
body: Mutability, the law of change and decay, is a major Renaissance theme (Spenser's 'Mutabilitie Cantos') and a recurrent one in Shelley. His short poem 'Mutability' ('We are as clouds that veil the midnight moon'), published with Alastor in 1816, ends 'Nought may endure but Mutability'. Here doubt (intellectual uncertainty), chance (lack of providence) and mutability define a world without a guaranteed metaphysical order, the condition the Hymn accepts as its starting point.

title: strings of some still instrument
short: The Aeolian harp, whose strings sound when the wind passes over them: an emblem of the mind played on by external power.
body: The image is of the wind-harp or Aeolian harp, a stringed box placed in a window, which sounds when the breeze crosses it. It was a favourite Romantic emblem of the passive, receptive mind, most famously in Coleridge's 'The Eolian Harp' (1795). Shelley returns to it in 'A Defence of Poetry' and the 'Ode to the West Wind' ('Make me thy lyre'). 'Still' (silent until the wind comes) stresses that the instrument has no music of its own: grace and truth come only when the Spirit's light visits.

title: Love, Hope, and Self-esteem
short: Here a virtue: justified self-respect, as in Milton, not vanity.
body: Shelley pairs Self-esteem with Love and Hope, as if a secular version of the theological virtues (faith, hope and charity) in 1 Corinthians 13. The word is positive, meaning a just valuation of oneself; editors compare Raphael's advice to Adam in Paradise Lost 8, that nothing profits more than 'self-esteem, grounded on just and right'. These states, too, are inconstant: they 'like clouds depart / And come'.

title: Man were immortal, and omnipotent
short: If the Spirit dwelt permanently in the human heart, humanity would be godlike: a strikingly humanist claim.
body: The conditional ('Man were immortal... Didst thou... Keep... firm state within his heart') is the poem's boldest statement. Divinity is relocated from heaven into the human mind: what makes gods is not a separate being but the constant presence of beauty, love and hope. The 'glorious train' pictures the Spirit as a monarch with a retinue holding 'firm state' (court) in the heart, a contrast with the inconstant visits of stanza 1. Critics read this as an early form of the meliorist vision of Prometheus Unbound.

title: Thou messenger of sympathies
short: The Spirit carries the shared feelings that pass, waxing and waning, between lovers.
body: 'Sympathies' in Shelley's usage means affinities and fellow-feeling, the emotional bonds between people. The Spirit is their messenger (Greek angelos, 'angel', means messenger, so the phrase quietly secularizes an angelic role). 'Wax and wane' compares the coming and going of love in lovers' eyes to the phases of the moon. Shelley's essay 'On Love' (written c. 1818, published posthumously) develops the idea of love as a sympathy seeking its counterpart.

title: Like darkness to a dying flame
short: A paradoxical simile: as a flame shows brightest against darkness, the Spirit nourishes thought by contrast; the image has puzzled readers.
body: The Spirit is 'to human thought... nourishment, / Like darkness to a dying flame'. Darkness does not literally feed a flame, so readers have offered several explanations: a flame appears most brilliant against darkness, so the Spirit sets off and intensifies thought; or the image is of a dying candle that seems to flare as night closes in. Some critics regard the simile as a deliberately unsettling paradox, consistent with a Power that is 'unknown and awful'. Editors note the difficulty without settling it.

title: While yet a boy I sought for ghosts
short: Autobiographical: Shelley's boyhood attempts at necromancy and ghost-raising, recalled by his biographers Hogg and Medwin.
body: The fifth stanza turns to personal narrative. Shelley's friends and biographers Thomas Jefferson Hogg (an Oxford friend) and Thomas Medwin (a cousin and schoolfellow) describe his youthful fascination with chemistry, magic and attempts to raise spirits. 'Hopes of high talk with the departed dead' refers to such necromantic experiments, influenced by gothic fiction. The 'poisonous names' are the names of demons or the spells of superstition, and perhaps also the religious teaching fed to children; the boy calls on them in vain.

title: I called on poisonous names with which our youth is fed
short: The names of supernatural beings taught in childhood, which Shelley regards as harmful; the target may include orthodox religion.
body: The line links the boy's invocation of spirits to what 'our youth is fed', implying that the names come from nursery superstition and religious instruction alike. Read with l. 27, it extends Shelley's scepticism from ghosts to the vocabulary of Christianity. The metaphor of feeding on poison also contrasts with the Spirit's true 'nourishment' in l. 44. Editors note that Shelley's attack is cautious enough to have been printed by Hunt in 1817.

title: I shrieked, and clasped my hands in ecstasy!
short: The moment of revelation: a secular conversion experience, described with physical abandon.
body: The Spirit's shadow falls suddenly in spring, not when sought but when the boy was musing on life. The response (shrieking, clasping the hands) imitates the language of evangelical conversion narratives, but the revelation is of beauty, not of God. 'Ecstasy' (Greek ekstasis, standing outside oneself) suggests rapture beyond the self. Some readers find the line overwrought; others see its awkwardness as a mark of sincerity. The structure, a childhood epiphany followed by a vow, parallels Wordsworth's dedication scene in The Prelude Book 4, though Shelley could not have read that poem, which was published in 1850.

anchor: I vowed that I would dedicate
title: I vowed that I would dedicate my powers
short: The poet's lifelong vow of dedication to the Spirit, a secular equivalent of a religious vocation.
body: The sixth stanza converts the experience into a vocation: like a priest or knight, the poet dedicates his 'powers' to the Spirit and asks whether he has kept the vow. The 'phantoms of a thousand hours' are his past selves or past studies, called from their graves as witnesses, in contrast to the ghosts he once tried to raise. Shelley's sense of a dedicated life also appears in the Dedication to Laon and Cythna (1817), which recalls a similar youthful moment of resolve.

title: visioned bowers / Of studious zeal or love's delight
short: Imagined retreats in which the poet has studied or loved through the night.
body: 'Visioned' means seen in a vision, imagined, and 'bowers' are secluded arbours, a romance word. The hours have 'Outwatched with me the envious night', staying awake until dawn in study or love; the night is 'envious' because it seeks to end or overshadow these pleasures. The lines suggest that the poet's devotion has been sustained by both intellectual labour and erotic love, which Shelley sees as two modes of the same pursuit of beauty.

title: O awful LOVELINESS
short: A second name for the Spirit; joined with 'awful' it fuses the beautiful and the sublime.
body: Eighteenth-century aesthetics, especially Burke's Philosophical Enquiry (1757), distinguished the beautiful (small, smooth, pleasing) from the sublime (vast, terrifying, awe-inspiring). Shelley's oxymoron 'awful LOVELINESS' unites them, as the opening 'awful shadow' did. The hope expressed here is political as well as personal: that the Spirit would free 'This world from its dark slavery', anticipating the revolutionary hopes of Laon and Cythna and Prometheus Unbound.

title: The day becomes more solemn and serene
short: The final stanza turns to autumn and afternoon, echoing the close of Wordsworth's Immortality Ode.
body: As noon passes and autumn arrives, the day gains a harmony and lustre 'not heard or seen' in summer. Critics have long compared Wordsworth's 'Ode: Intimations of Immortality' (1807), whose last stanza finds a 'sober colouring' in the clouds round the setting sun and a 'philosophic mind' replacing youthful vision. Shelley similarly asks that his mature life be granted the 'calm' that the Spirit's visits once brought in youth. The difference is that Shelley's consolation does not rest on a belief in pre-existence or immortality.

title: on my passive youth
short: His young self was receptive rather than active: the Spirit 'descended' upon him like truth from nature.
body: 'Passive' implies receptivity, being acted upon, the condition of the wind-harp in stanza 3. The simile 'like the truth / Of nature' suggests a natural revelation rather than a supernatural one. Shelley now asks that this power 'supply' his 'onward life' with calm: the movement from youthful passivity to adult dedication is the poem's narrative arc. The prayer is modest: not for renewed ecstasy but for the autumnal serenity described at the opening of the stanza, a mature steadiness grounded in the earlier visitations.

title: To fear himself, and love all human kind
short: The Spirit's lesson is ethical: self-distrust and universal love, not worship of a god.
body: The poem closes by defining its worshipper as one bound by the Spirit's 'spells' to 'fear himself, and love all human kind'. 'Fear himself' probably means to be wary of one's own capacity for selfishness and evil, and perhaps to revere the divinity potentially within oneself; 'love all human kind' recalls the second great commandment (Matthew 22:39) without its first, the love of God. Many readers take the ending as the humanist core of Shelley's faith in beauty as a moral force.
